articles.title: Sperm counts may be falling, but humans are unlikely to run out
articles.author: Michael Carroll, Reader  / Associate Professor in Reproductive Science, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: For years, alarming headlines have warned that sperm counts are plummeting and humanity could be heading towards a fertility crisis. But new research suggests the picture is considerably more complicated.

A study published in September 2026 examined semen samples from 8,320 young Danish men collected over 26 years. Rather than finding a steady decline, the researchers reported that sperm counts had remained relatively stable between 1996 and 2022, with some modest improvements in recent years.
That doesn’t mean everything is fine. More than a third of the men had at least one measure of semen quality below World Health Organization reference levels.

These findings contrast with an influential 2017 study reporting that sperm concentration among men in Western countries had fallen by more than half between 1973 and 2011. When the researchers expanded their analysis in 2022, they concluded that sperm counts were declining worldwide, with the rate of decline accelerating.

As a reproductive scientist specialising in sperm biology and male fertility, I’ve spent much of my career studying how sperm function and what influences their quality. In my book, Your Nuts: The Science of How They Work and What It Means for Your Fertility, I explore what sperm counts can tell us about reproductive health, and more importantly, what they cannot

So what is actually happening to human sperm numbers? Are they falling worldwide, or do trends differ between populations? And perhaps most importantly, what do sperm counts really tell us about male fertility?
Are sperm counts still falling?
While the results from the 2017 study appear alarming, more recent studies have continued to produce very different results.

A review published online in 2024 analysed research involving almost 12,000 US men. Its main analyses found no statistically significant decline in sperm concentration between 1970 and 2018. However, a modest decline emerged when researchers adjusted for both geographical region and fertility status.

Another 2024 study examined semen samples from prospective sperm donors in Denmark. Sperm concentration and total sperm count remained relatively stable between 2017 and 2022, although sperm motility, or how well sperm move, declined.

Between 2019 and 2022, the concentration of moving sperm fell by 16%, while the total number of moving sperm per ejaculate declined by 22%. This is important because sperm movement is another factor influencing the likelihood of conception.

Meanwhile, researchers in Ireland analysed more than 18,000 semen samples from over 15,000 men attending a fertility clinic between 2008 and 2023. They found that median sperm concentration increased by almost 23%, from 57 million to 70 million sperm per millilitre. However, the proportion of samples containing very low concentrations of sperm, or no sperm at all, remained relatively unchanged.

Taken together, these studies suggest that trends in semen quality can vary considerably between populations and regions. And this means that the question of whether sperm counts are declining globally is far from settled.

There are also important limitations. Studies involving sperm donors or fertility clinic patients may not reflect the wider population. Meanwhile, research examining long-term trends often relies on semen samples collected at different times and locations, sometimes using different methods.
These differences make comparisons difficult. The newer studies cannot simply cancel out the larger global analyses, but they demonstrate why interpreting changes in sperm counts requires caution.
Sperm count isn’t the same as fertility
There is another problem with the extinction narrative: sperm count alone cannot tell us whether a man is fertile.

Semen analysis also considers sperm movement and shape, alongside other characteristics. Although very low sperm concentrations can reduce the likelihood of conception, they do not necessarily make pregnancy impossible.

Research into male contraception illustrates this. In trials of hormonal contraceptives, pregnancies occurred even when sperm concentrations had been suppressed to very low levels, including three million sperm per millilitre or less. Although the likelihood of conception was greatly reduced, it was not eliminated.
This demonstrates why sperm numbers cannot be treated as a simple dividing line between fertility and infertility.
There is also enormous natural variation in the number of sperm an individual man produces, including differences between samples collected from the same person.

In one study involving 329 men, researchers found considerable variation in semen measurements over time. Relying on a single sample could sometimes give a misleading picture of an individual’s semen quality.
This is one reason current UK clinical guidance recommends repeat semen analysis when an initial result is abnormal.

It also illustrates the difficulty of determining whether sperm counts have fallen over several decades, particularly when the studies involved different populations and methods of collecting and analysing samples.
None of this means we should dismiss concerns about male reproductive health.

Male infertility is a significant health issue, and research into the environmental, lifestyle and medical factors that influence sperm production remains important. As the World Health Organization acknowledges, infertility affects millions of people worldwide, and male reproductive health deserves greater attention.
But the evidence doesn’t support the idea that humanity is about to disappear because we’re running out of sperm.
The dramatic headlines may have overstated the science. What they achieved, however, was to shine a much-needed light on male fertility, and that is a conversation worth having.

articles.title: Scientists find way to repair heart damage after a heart attack
articles.author: David C. Gaze, Senior Lecturer in Chemical Pathology, University of Westminster
paras: Every year, millions of people worldwide suffer a heart attack. Thanks to advances in emergency treatment, many now survive an event that might once have been fatal. Yet surviving a heart attack is not necessarily the end of the story. The damage can be permanent, increasing the risk of heart failure, breathlessness and a poorer quality of life.

Researchers have developed an experimental treatment that could change how we approach recovery after a heart attack. Rather than simply protecting the remaining heart muscle, the new approach aims to encourage the heart to repair itself. So far, it has only been tested in mice.

The findings, published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research, describe how modified messenger RNA (mRNA) can encourage heart muscle cells to multiply, potentially improving the heart’s ability to pump blood.
Although this is still early-stage research, the study offers the tantalising possibility that one day we might be able to encourage the adult human heart to regenerate damaged muscle.
Why the heart struggles to repair itself

A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow through a coronary artery is significantly reduced or even fully blocked. Without oxygen, the cells of the heart muscle begin to die. These specialised cells, called cardiomyocytes, are responsible for the continuous contractions of the heart muscle, which pumps blood around the body to our vital organs.

Unlike skin or liver tissue, the adult human heart has limited capacity to replace damaged cells. Instead, dead muscle is largely replaced by fibrous scar tissue. Although this scar helps maintain the heart’s structural integrity, it cannot contract like healthy muscle.
The consequence is a heart that may become progressively weaker, sometimes leading to heart failure.

Modern treatments, such as procedures to reopen blocked arteries, medication and supervised exercise programmes, have greatly improved survival. But they cannot replace heart muscle that has already died.

During the early development of the heart, the cardiomyocytes divide, allowing the heart muscle to grow. Shortly after birth, most mammalian cardiomyocytes largely lose this ability. The researchers investigated whether they could restart this process by making heart muscle cells produce two proteins, called Myc and cyclin T1.

Myc switches on genes involved in cell growth and division, while cyclin T1 helps activate the machinery cells need to multiply. Together, the proteins can encourage mature heart muscle cells to start dividing again.

The researchers used modified mRNA to give heart muscle cells instructions for making the two proteins. This is the same basic technology used in COVID vaccines, which deliver temporary genetic instructions to cells to make a protein that trains the immune system to recognise the virus.

Importantly, mRNA does not need to alter a cell’s DNA. Instead, it provides temporary instructions that are naturally broken down. This temporary activity is particularly important when stimulating cell growth because uncontrolled cell growth is the basis of cancer.
What happened in the damaged hearts?
The researchers tested their approach in mice following experimentally induced heart attacks.

The researchers injected the modified mRNA directly into the damaged hearts of mice that had suffered heart attacks. The treatment activated genes involved in cell division, prompting heart muscle cells to start multiplying. Crucially, the treated mice also showed improvements in heart function.
After 28 days, the treated mice had lost less pumping ability than untreated mice. They also had more heart muscle tissue.
In a longer experiment, improvements in heart function were still evident 12 weeks after treatment.

These findings suggest that temporarily activating the heart’s growth machinery may help restore some of the function lost following injury. However, the treatment did not consistently reduce scar tissue. This suggests that the heart’s improved pumping ability did not necessarily mean damaged muscle had been fully replaced.
One of the most important findings concerns safety. Myc is a powerful regulator of cell growth and is also associated with cancer when its activity becomes uncontrolled.
Activating Myc and cyclin T1 widely throughout the damaged heart could be dangerous. In one experiment, several mice developed severe illness or died.

Restricting activation to a smaller region of heart muscle surrounding the initial injury produced a much more favourable response. The findings highlight a major challenge: researchers must find a way to stimulate heart muscle cells to divide without triggering uncontrolled growth elsewhere in the heart.
Encouragingly, no tumours were observed during the reported follow-up of mice receiving the localised treatment. However, longer studies will be essential to establish safety.

There are substantial obstacles before this approach could be tested routinely in patients. The treatment has not yet been shown to regenerate damaged human hearts. Researchers must work out how to deliver the treatment safely, find the right dose and check for complications such as abnormal heart rhythms and uncontrolled cell growth. Still, the findings are an important advance in regenerative cardiovascular medicine.

For decades, the emphasis after a heart attack has been on preventing further damage and helping the surviving heart muscle work more efficiently. This research points towards a different ambition: replacing some of the muscle that has already been lost.

If future studies demonstrate that the approach is both safe and effective in humans, treating a heart attack might one day involve not only restoring blood flow, but also giving the heart the instructions it needs to repair itself.

articles.title: Spermmaxxing: the science behind ice packs, red light and abstinence
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Some men are taking ice packs into saunas to protect their testicles from the heat. Others are shining red lights on their groins or eating raw butter in the hope of improving their sperm. There are even organised sperm races, with competitors and spectators.

Welcome to spermmaxxing, the latest online trend promising men ways to boost their sperm count and quality. It brings male fertility into the world of internet self-optimisation, where almost any part of the body can become a project.
But do these techniques actually work? And what can sperm count tell someone about their chances of becoming a parent?
In this episode of the Strange Health podcast, I investigate the claims with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Michael Carroll, a reproductive scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University and former NHS clinical embryologist. He helps us explore what the evidence says about sperm health, and where online advice gets ahead of the science.
Why an ice pack is not a fertility plan

Some spermmaxxing ideas begin with a grain of biological truth. Testicles generally need to be cooler than the rest of the body for sperm production to function normally, and repeated exposure to high temperatures may affect sperm quality. But that doesn’t establish that strapping an ice pack to your groin while sitting in a sauna will improve fertility.

Red-light treatments are also being promoted online. Researchers have investigated how particular kinds of light affect sperm in laboratory conditions. Evidence that devices used at home improve men’s chances of fathering a child, however, is lacking. As for a diet built around raw butter and animal products, an impressive-looking plate is no substitute for clinical evidence.

The interest in spermmaxxing is partly fuelled by reports of declining sperm counts. A major review found that average sperm counts fell in the populations it studied over several decades. But a sperm count on its own cannot tell you whether you can conceive. Doctors may also look at how well sperm move and their shape, alongside other aspects of reproductive health.
What happens when fertility becomes a competition?

Dan and I also take a detour into the history of sperm science, beginning with Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who observed moving sperm through a microscope in 1677. Almost 350 years later, sperm racing has turned microscopic movement into an actual spectator event.

There’s a serious subject beneath the spectacle. Male infertility can be distressing, and some causes need medical assessment rather than lifestyle experiments. We explore conditions such as varicocele, enlarged veins around the testicles, and azoospermia, when semen contains no sperm, as well as the treatments that may help.
Listen to the episode to discover what spermmaxxing gets right, where its claims fall short and what men concerned about their fertility can do instead.

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
articles.author: Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago
paras: The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000. A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17.
Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025, as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world. What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95%. But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine.

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963. The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective. A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children. After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99%, and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated.

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.
So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine, measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases.

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia, leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.
In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it.
A surge of outbreaks – and deaths

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized.

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak, which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status.
Fertile ground for misinformation
When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010, and its author lost his medical license. But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day, even though studies that included millions of children have found no link.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience.
Federal policy fuels further confusion
Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots, which are not sold in the United States. There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment, not a cure or vaccine substitute.
Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26. Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2%.

Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.
Adult immunity also has gaps: Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission. That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.
But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.

The Department of Health and Human Services blames current vaccination gaps on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that the agency would not make any changes in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status.
Additionally, orders like August’s about the MMR vaccine, and revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations, are weakening vaccination efforts.

Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible has been substantially weakened.
So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.

articles.title: Why does your body store fat in your butt?
articles.author: Cara Ocobock, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, University of Notre Dame
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why does your body store fat in your butt? - Ellen, age 8, Cambridge, Massachusetts
Have you ever wondered why some parts of your body are firm, like your elbows, while other areas, like your butt, are squishier?
The difference is due to what scientists call fat distribution, and researchers are still trying to understand why bodies store fat in some places but not in others.
All animals have fat in their bodies, even insects. Bears even put on up to 400 pounds (180 kilograms) of additional body fat, the equivalent of 544 large cheese pizzas, to survive hibernation.
Fat is an important and constantly changing part of all bodies, including those of humans and our evolutionary ancestors.
Fat, also called adipose tissue, is one kind of connective tissue that helps hold your body together.

For a long time, scientists thought that adipose tissue was mainly a storage place for the extra energy your body doesn’t use from the food you eat. While fat is a great source of stored energy, it also has many other functions. There are even different kinds of fat.

Visceral fat serves as a sort of protective bubble wrap, surrounding and filling in the spaces between your internal organs. Subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat between your skin and your muscle that you can pinch, is a protective cushion and helps to keep you warm by insulating you like a coat.
Fat also produces and responds to hormones, a type of chemical messenger, to regulate how your body uses energy and to tell you when you are hungry or full.
Different kinds of fat also have different jobs. White fat is the kind of fat most people are familiar with and performs the functions mentioned above.
You may be less familiar with brown fat, which is brown because it contains a lot of mitochondria: the parts of your cells that produce the energy your body needs to perform all its functions.

Not all animals have brown fat, but humans do. Scientists know that brown fat performs a special function to heat your body when you get cold. It doesn’t store energy, like white fat does, to help your body move.

When you were a baby, you had a lot of brown fat along your torso to help keep you warm because your body wasn’t mature enough to maintain your body temperature. As you grow older, you have less brown fat. It is only located just above your collar bone and along your major deep blood vessels, like your aorta.
Why do humans store fat where we do?

Researchers don’t know enough yet about brown fat to know why it is in just a few parts of the body. It is possible that it’s near the neck and around major blood vessels to help insulate the blood and keep overall body temperature in a healthy warm range.
As for white fat, there appear to be three main factors that determine where your fat gets stored: genetics, hormones and age.
Certain genes direct fat to accumulate in the butt, while other genes tell it to collect on the torso.

Hormones like estrogen, which affects almost every system in all bodies but is typically higher in females, direct more subcutaneous fat to gather in the butt, thighs and backs of the arms. Cortisol, the stress hormone, seems to direct visceral fat to accumulate in the belly area.

But why isn’t fat evenly distributed throughout the body? Well, having a lot of fat around your elbows and knees would limit your ability to bend your arms and legs. Storing a lot of fat around your head would possibly put your brain at risk of overheating. Other parts of your body, like hips, butts, breasts and thighs, don’t have these risks – maybe that’s why we store fat there.
Why do people have fat at all?

Don’t be fooled: A lot of animals that look fat, like a hippopotamus, actually aren’t. Hippos only have around 2% body fat, the percentage of how much of your body mass comes from fat; while the average human woman has over 30% body fat.

In the rest of the animal kingdom, biologists typically only see a lot of body fat among hibernating or marine mammals. For the hibernators, the fat serves as energy storage for long, cold winters. For marine mammals like seals and whales, that extra fat is like a giant puffy coat helping to keep them warm in the cold depths of the ocean.
Humans do not hibernate, nor do we live in the ocean, so why do we have a lot more fat than all other primates and most mammals?

Anthropologists like me, who study how the human body has evolved over time, think it has to do with the lifestyle of our evolutionary ancestors who had to gather and hunt to survive. Gathering and hunting were not always reliable food sources. We think our ancestors developed the ability to put on extra fat as a food insurance policy. When food was difficult to find, they could rely on their extra fat stores to carry them through until food became available again.
Researchers are still trying to determine when this extra fat storage evolved. We have one line of evidence from small stone figures known as Gravettian statues.
These ancient statues from 25,000 to 28,000 years ago depict feminine figures who carry a lot of extra body fat. Archaeologists have found them all throughout Europe and Russia.

The way the ancient artists depicted fat on these figures matches how fat looks on bodies today. This accuracy has led researchers to believe that the makers of the Gravettian statues knew how individuals with greater body fat actually looked, meaning at least some people at this time did put on a lot of extra fat.

Europe and Russia back then were much colder than they are today, supporting the idea that our ancestors would have needed the extra fat to get through the extremely cold winters when food was harder to find.
So, the next time you poke at your butt fat, remember that fat is a really important part of our bodies, performs lots of different functions, and is likely evolutionarily ancient for us humans.

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: Treating iron deficiency: the everyday factors that affect how your supplements work
articles.author: Hal Drakesmith, Professor of Iron Biology, University of Oxford
paras: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting around 2 billion people. Yet many people may not even realise they have low iron for months or even years.

This is a concern, as untreated iron deficiency can have widespread effects on the body. It can lead to anaemia — a condition which can cause tiredness, shortness or breath, heart palpitations, headaches and even difficulty concentrating.
This is why it’s key for those diagnosed with an iron deficiency to take measures to top up their iron stores.

Iron deficiency is typically treated by taking a daily supplement. But while this sounds straightforward, a number of factors and even everyday habits can interfere with how well your supplement is absorbed.

Iron plays an important role in the body. It supports our cells and is key in many bodily processes – including immune function and growth. Iron helps the body to make and repair DNA, generate energy and metabolise cholesterol. This is why an iron deficiency can have such widespread effects on our health.
Iron deficiency can occur for any number of reasons.

Infants and children may be at risk of iron deficiency because of their rapid growth and development, which means they have a high demand for iron. This demand can often outstrip the amount they’re getting in their diet.

Women are also at greater risk of iron deficiency. Pre-menopausal women lose iron every month when they menstruate, which can be challenging to replenish. Pregnancy also dramatically increases iron requirements, as both mother and the growing foetus need iron.
In the elderly iron deficiency can be driven by slow blood loss from the intestine, poor appetite or chronic illness.
Poor diet may also contribute to iron deficiency – particularly diets that are low in red meat or iron-fortified foods.

Another important factor to consider is inflammation. Our iron levels are controlled by a hormone called hepcidin. Hepcidin ensures we only absorb as much iron from our diet as we need. In people who have an iron deficiency, hepcidin levels fall to allow us to take in more iron and restore our iron reserves.

However, inflammation (the body’s reaction to an infection or disease) switches on hepcidin to a high level. The result of this is a decrease in the amount of iron available to make red blood cells. If inflammation becomes chronic, it can cause anaemia.
Figuring out the root cause of your iron deficiency is key so you can properly address the problem.
The only way to accurately diagnose iron deficiency is by having a blood test done. This will measure levels of a specific protein called ferritin.
Ferritin’s job is to safely store iron atoms. Ferritin increases with the amount of iron that needs to be stored. So low ferritin is an accurate indicator for iron deficiency.
If you have been diagnosed with low iron, there are several ways to combat deficiency.

The first strategy involves changing your diet so you’re eating more iron-rich foods. This can include red meat, lentils, fortified cereals and leafy greens. You should ideally pair any iron-rich foods with vitamin C to aid iron absorption.
However, this may not efficiently correct iron deficiency if your iron levels are very low or if you have a problem absorbing iron from your diet.

Oral iron tablets are another way of topping up levels as these provide much more iron. Current guidelines recommend a dosage of 65mg of iron (or 200mg of ferrous sulfate) daily or every other day to treat iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia.

But a problem with supplements is that only a fraction of the iron in each tablet is typically absorbed. Side-effects can also include nausea and constipation, which may discourage continued treatment.

To improve how iron supplements work, try taking one tablet per day on an empty stomach to aid absorption – or wait until two hours after you’ve eaten. You should also try to take it with orange juice or another source of vitamin C. If the supplements bother your stomach, take them every other day or consume with food.
Avoid taking calcium tablets at the same time as iron as calcium can decrease iron absorption. You should ideally wait two hours after taking an iron supplement before taking calcium.

Tea and coffee may also affect iron absorption, as these contain tannins – molecules which make it harder for the body to absorb iron. Phytates, compounds which are found in seeds and grains, can also inhibit iron absorption.

You will likely need to take iron tablets for several months to correct iron deficiency anaemia and bolster your body’s iron stores. Another ferritin check will indicate if the iron tablets are working.

If iron supplements just aren’t working or if your iron levels are seriously low, intravenous iron treatments may be the best option as these bypass the intestine. They provide a large dose of iron that is then be released over time to replenish stores and help production of red blood cells.

Iron deficiency remains a substantial health issue worldwide. But advances in our understanding of its causes and effects, more public awareness of the problem and improved methods of iron replenishment mean that it’s increasingly a treatable condition.

articles.title: A cancer drug is being touted online as a way to grow taller – what you need to know
articles.author: Justin Stebbing, Professor of Biomedical Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: A cancer drug linked to rapid growth spurts in children has caught the attention of teenagers looking to gain an extra few inches in height.

Erdafitinib, a medicine designed to treat advanced cancer, has been linked to extraordinary growth spurts in children receiving treatment for brain tumours. Reports of these effects have fuelled interest among people seeking to maximise their height – so-called “heightmaxxing”, though it’s unclear how many are actually taking the drug. However, the trend is visible enough online that TikTok has banned some accounts from promoting it.
However, the same treatment that appears to stimulate height can also interfere with normal skeletal development, potentially causing permanent damage.

Erdafitinib is a targeted cancer drug approved for treating certain patients with advanced bladder cancer. It is also used experimentally for certain types of brain tumour in children. It blocks a family of proteins called fibroblast growth factor receptors, or FGFRs.

These receptors act like molecular switches, controlling how cells grow, divide and survive. In some cancers, genetic changes leave these switches permanently on, causing cells to multiply uncontrollably. Erdafitinib interferes with these signals, slowing cancer cell growth.

Unlike conventional chemotherapy, which affects many rapidly dividing cells, targeted therapies are designed to interfere with specific molecular pathways. But these pathways are rarely exclusive to cancer.
FGFRs also work in healthy tissues, including the eyes, skin and, crucially, developing bones. Blocking them can therefore affect much more than the tumour.

The link to height lies in how bones grow. During childhood and adolescence, long bones contain regions of cartilage near their ends called growth plates. Cartilage cells in these plates multiply and enlarge before gradually being replaced by bone. This process lengthens the arms, legs and spine.
One receptor, FGFR3, helps control this process. Surprisingly, it acts as a brake rather than an accelerator on bone growth.
When FGFR3 is overactive, cartilage growth is restricted, as in achondroplasia, the most common cause of disproportionate short stature.

Scientists have therefore investigated whether reducing FGFR3 activity might encourage bone growth. Treatments targeting this pathway are already being studied or used for certain skeletal disorders. Erdafitinib blocks several FGFR proteins, including FGFR3, raising the possibility that it could release the biological brakes on height.
But stimulating bone growth and producing a healthy, proportionate skeleton are not necessarily the same thing.

The excitement stems largely from a couple of cases. Researchers in Vienna described two children with brain tumours who experienced unexpectedly rapid growth while taking the drug. Their growth did not appear to be explained by growth hormone or puberty, which suggests the drug was directly affecting skeletal development.
An even more dramatic case involved a 15-year-old boy treated with erdafitinib for a brain tumour. Over about nine months, he grew 14.3 centimetres – far more than would be expected in that time.
However, the rapid growth came with serious skeletal abnormalities, including spinal deformities that needed corrective surgery.

These reports are scientifically important, but they involve very small numbers of seriously ill children, often receiving other treatments. They cannot tell us whether erdafitinib would safely increase the final height of healthy adolescents, or whether the extra growth would be sustained, proportionate and accompanied by normal bone strength.

Taking erdafitinib to grow taller is dangerous for several reasons. Bones, muscles, ligaments and joints must develop together to maintain strength and alignment. Accelerating one part without the others could result in deformities, abnormal spinal curvature or poor bone mineralisation.

The drug also has significant side-effects unrelated to height, including a rise in phosphate levels in the blood. Phosphate is essential for healthy bones, but excessive levels can contribute to abnormal mineral deposits in tissues. Erdafitinib can also cause serious eye problems, which may threaten vision.

In cancer medicine, such risks may be justified when a drug offers the chance of controlling a life-threatening disease. For an otherwise healthy teenager hoping to be slightly taller, the balance between benefit and harm is entirely different.

Social media discussions also tend to overlook a basic biological limit. Once puberty is complete, the growth plates normally fuse, and the long bones can no longer lengthen. There is no credible evidence that erdafitinib can make a fully grown adult taller, whatever the dose.
The high price of heightmaxxing
The popularity of heightmaxxing and other forms of maxxing reflects a broader cultural obsession with appearance, particularly among young men.

Social media increasingly presents height, muscularity and facial features as things that can, and perhaps should, be optimised. In online communities where a few extra centimetres are portrayed as the difference between romantic success and failure, the temptation to experiment with unproven treatments can be powerful.

The effects of erdafitinib on bone growth may eventually contribute to medical advances. Understanding how FGFR signalling controls skeletal development could help researchers develop treatments for children with specific growth disorders. But turning an unexpected side-effect into a safe treatment requires rigorous clinical trials, careful dosing and long-term monitoring.

For now, the lesson from erdafitinib is clear: a medicine that can make bones grow faster does not necessarily make them grow better. For anyone risking their eyesight, skeletal health and potentially permanent disability in pursuit of an extra inch or two, heightmaxxing could come at an extraordinarily high price.

articles.title: Astaxanthin supplements: what the science says about skin, exercise and your brain
articles.author: Mayur Ranchordas, Professor of Applied Sport Nutrition and Sport Nutrition Consultant, Sheffield Hallam University
paras: Smoother skin, sharper eyesight, better memory, stronger joints, improved athletic performance and even protection against ageing – astaxanthin is marketed as a supplement with an extraordinary range of health benefits. But how much of this promise is backed by evidence in people?

Astaxanthin is a reddish-orange pigment made mainly by microalgae. Salmon, prawns and other marine animals accumulate it through their diet, and flamingos get their colour in a similar way from foods rich in carotenoid pigments. It belongs to the same family as betacarotene, found in carrots and sweet potatoes, and lutein, found in spinach and kale.

Astaxanthin has attracted attention because it can act as an antioxidant, helping to protect cells against unstable molecules produced during normal metabolism, illness and exercise. This provides a plausible biological explanation for why astaxanthin might be useful. But a supplement that affects cells in a lab does not necessarily make people healthier, fitter or longer lived.

The best evidence is for skin. A review of 11 studies found that astaxanthin improved skin moisture and elasticity compared with a placebo. It found no clear reduction in wrinkle depth, and the benefits were largely confined to studies in healthy women.

Most of the trials were small and short, so it is hard to know whether the changes last. An improvement picked up by specialist equipment may also be invisible in the mirror. Astaxanthin is no substitute for protecting your skin from the sun.

Claims about recovery from exercise are on shakier ground. A review of 24 trials found that astaxanthin reduced markers of muscle damage after exercise. But there was no clear improvement in aerobic fitness, maximum power or time-trial performance.

A lower reading in a blood sample does not necessarily translate into less soreness or a quicker return to training. For most athletes, finishing a race faster or feeling ready for the next session counts for more than a small shift in a laboratory result.

The cognitive evidence is weaker still. An analysis of 11 trials involving 346 healthy participants found no clear improvement in reaction time and only a marginal effect on cognitive accuracy. That is a long way from showing that astaxanthin protects against dementia or age-related decline.

Claims about eyesight and heart health rest largely on plausible mechanisms and small studies. Astaxanthin can reach different tissues and may influence oxidative stress and inflammation, but a review found the evidence across these conditions limited and inconsistent.

Some studies in humans have reported improvements in cholesterol, blood sugar and other cardiovascular risk markers. Improving one measurement does not prove that a supplement prevents heart attacks or strokes, which would take much larger studies following people for several years.

Astaxanthin is also marketed for weight loss, sometimes with claims that it boosts fat burning. An analysis of nine clinical trials found no significant effect on body weight or body mass index. Taking a larger dose did not produce better results.

On safety, the short-term evidence is generally reassuring. Side-effects are usually mild and can include stomach discomfort and changes in stool colour. Because astaxanthin is a pigment, very high intakes may also give the skin a reddish tinge.

The European Food Safety Authority concluded that 8mg a day from supplements, alongside astaxanthin from food, was safe for adults. That does not show that larger doses are beneficial, or reveal what happens after years of daily use. Evidence is also limited for children and during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Astaxanthin is an interesting compound, and its effects on skin moisture and exercise-recovery markers deserve further research. The question for anyone considering it is whether a daily capsule will deliver a benefit you can see, feel or measure in everyday life. From what we know today, the science has not made that case.
Until larger, genuinely independent trials give stronger answers, the most noticeable effect may be on your wallet.

articles.title: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
articles.author: Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia
paras: The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.
The Conversation asked Dr. Andrew Wolf, a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the lead authors of the new guidelines, to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.
What are the new screening recommendations?

The biggest change is that we are making a proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer. Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.
Our new recommendations vary by age and by a person’s risk of developing prostate cancer.

For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.

People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.

For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, decision-making around screening depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy.

For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group.

Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is less effective than the PSA test. The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.
Why were the screening guidelines updated?
The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer.
The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer or of being diagnosed with metastatic disease are actually greater than researchers previously thought.

At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including false positive PSA test results and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are unlikely to harm patients in the long-term.
Who is most at risk for prostate cancer?

Black men have an approximately two-thirds higher risk of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors.
Men with a family history of prostate cancer in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk.

There are also a number of genetic mutations, such as BRCA2, that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American Urological Association, have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations.
Why has the PSA test been so controversial?

For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, a U.S. study, found no benefit to screening; the other, a European study, found only a relatively small benefit.

However, it later became clear that the U.S. study was seriously flawed in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up.

Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening.

After researchers followed patients for over two decades in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer.

This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as mammography for breast cancer. And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.
Why are there differences in guidelines?

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s last update in 2018, it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.
The task force has been in the process of updating those guidelines over the past several years. It is possible that their update will more closely align with that of the American Cancer Society.

I do think we have both sufficient evidence of benefit and sufficient reduction of the risks to now proactively recommend screening. Where the two guidelines do align is that both recommend that patients be informed of the benefits, risks and limitations of prostate cancer screening so they know what they’re getting into.

It is likely that our new screening recommendations will be covered by most insurers. However, patients may have out-of-pocket costs for further testing their doctor orders as a result of an abnormal PSA level.
What would you say to people hesitant about screening?
Even though the benefits far outweigh the risks, there may be legitimate reasons why some people may not wish to undergo screening.

Some people might want to avoid the possibility of needing to get a prostate biopsy, which is how clinicians diagnose prostate cancer if a patient has an elevated PSA and an abnormal follow-up MRI scan or biomarker test. Prostate biopsies are uncomfortable, and they may cause some bleeding or occasionally an infection.

Some people may want to avoid the possibility of needing to undergo active surveillance if they discover they have a tumor that isn’t growing aggressively. Active surveillance involves periodic biopsies, MRI scans or both, which can be inconvenient and anxiety-provoking.
Some people may want to avoid the potential side effects of treating early-stage prostate cancer with surgery or radiation, which can cause sexual, urinary and bowel problems.
Forgoing screening, however, also means forgoing the opportunity to find cancer at its earliest stages, when the chance for a cure is very high.

Andrew Wolf serves as Chair of the American Cancer Society's Guideline Development Group. This is a volunteer position. Opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead
articles.author: Robert Brehm, PhD Candidate in Politics, University of Virginia
paras: Candidates tied to the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement suffered a series of electoral defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, raising questions about MAHA’s political future.

Despite its name, MAHA has become a controversial force in American health politics. While the movement calls for healthier food, increased physical activity and greater corporate transparency, prominent figures within it have also challenged established scientific evidence, especially on vaccines.

Some commentators and critics have described the defeat of MAHA-aligned candidates like Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn as a “brutal election night wipeout.” Others have asked whether MAHA is “dying.”

Yet many Americans still support MAHA and the policies it champions. Its supporters also continue to hold powerful positions in the Trump administration – like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Kyle Diamantas, acting commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – even as a new Congress prepares to take office in January 2027.

We are political scientists who study public opinion on healthcare policy. We see MAHA’s electoral losses as a political setback, not a death sentence. The movement’s influence extends beyond its candidates and the elections they contest.
MAHA’s electoral losses came amid a potentially generational swing toward Democrats across the country,

More than half the 24 gubernatorial and Congressional candidates endorsed by MAHA’s political action committee, MAHA Action, lost their election bids. These included Lahn, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Vic Mellor in Rhode Island. Others, like incumbent Representative Anna Paulina Luna, R-FL, won by less than 1% in a district that she won by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024.

Lahn’s defeat stands out as a major loss. Lahn, a farmer who railed against pesticides on the campaign trail and promised to ban COVID-19 vaccinations in Iowa, was endorsed by Kennedy. Lahn has been described by some as a model MAHA candidate and received over US$1 million in campaign contributions from MAHA Action.
Public support remains strong

But the movement’s poor showing at the ballot box does not mean that some of MAHA’s ideas are unpopular among Americans. A May 2026 poll conducted by the health policy organization KFF found that 41% of American adults supported MAHA, including many Democrats and independents.

Many Americans also share MAHA’s concerns about food safety. According to KFF, 75% of Americans believe the government does too little to regulate chemical additives in food, while 64% say the same about agricultural pesticides.

Yet the popularity of MAHA policies did little to help MAHA-backed candidates win in the first election cycle where MAHA-aligned candidates were on the ballot. Following the midterm elections, some MAHA activists moved to blame President Donald Trump for failing to fulfill promises on these issues.

One prime example: In a postelection episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals. Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one postelection poll finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office.

Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story. Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered lowering healthcare costs their top health priority. By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety. Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats. Most MAHA supporters, however, continued to vote for Republicans.

Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand. Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates. Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies. MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy.
MAHA remains the status quo in Washington

Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington. Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention steers vaccine recommendations in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views. These efforts face growing scrutiny amid public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance and reports that he sought to remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics.

Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks. Following the election, he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”

MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress. Facing greater opposition, the administration may increasingly rely on executive actions, including executive orders, new federal regulations and agency reports, to advance its health policies. However, Congress can also investigate HHS decisions and use its control over federal spending to limit what the agency can do.

MAHA’s political future remains uncertain. Some supporters may gradually move toward Democrats, particularly those concerned about corporate influence, pharmaceutical industry accountability and food safety. These concerns cross partisan lines, giving Democrats an opportunity to appeal to voters dissatisfied with Trump but still supportive of MAHA’s priorities.

MAHA could also become a movement independent of Trump and MAGA. It could bring together Americans who care about health and wellness, distrust major institutions and oppose corporate influence over food and medicine. Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign attracted as much as 15% support among voters in July 2024. This showed that an alternative to the two major parties could attract substantial support.

Whether MAHA remains tied to Trump’s increasingly divided coalition will shape its future beyond his presidency. The frustrations and health concerns that fueled its rise among Americans have not disappeared.

articles.title: Early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood – new study
articles.author: Justin Stebbing, Professor of Biomedical Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: The most common type of ovarian cancer tends to grow quickly. It’s called high-grade serous ovarian cancer and often starts in a fallopian tube, one of the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries towards the womb.

The first changes can be so small that they’re usually found only when a specialist examines the tube under a microscope after surgery. Now, a new study suggests that some of those changes may leave a trace in the blood.

The researchers looked for a molecule called Tu-stroma in stored blood samples. They found higher levels in people with early cancer that had begun growing into nearby tissue. Levels were also higher in people with a tiny patch of abnormal cells still confined to the lining of the fallopian tube. This patch, known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (Stic for short), can be an early step towards this type of ovarian cancer. The next step is to follow people over time to find out when the signal first appears.

Ovarian cancer can cause symptoms such as persistent bloating and pain in the tummy or low down between the hips. Some people feel full after eating very little or need to pee more often. These symptoms are common in other conditions too. If they persist or keep coming back, it’s worth getting them checked by a GP.

When investigating symptoms, doctors may use a blood test for CA125, a protein whose level can rise when ovarian cancer is present. Other conditions can raise it too, including endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the womb lining grows elsewhere in the body. Some people with early ovarian cancer still have a low CA125 level. The UK has no routine screening programme to check people without symptoms for ovarian cancer.
What the researchers found

Tu-stroma is a type of RNA, one of the molecules cells use to control how they work. Earlier research showed that ovarian cancer cells can release Tu-stroma in tiny packages called extracellular vesicles. Think of these as microscopic parcels carrying messages from one cell to another. The researchers measured how much Tu-stroma these parcels were carrying in the blood.

They analysed samples from 506 people, including 43 with Stic alone. In a separate group used to check how well the test worked, it picked up Stic in about 92% of those who had it. The test showed no signs of Stic in about 98% of people in the healthy comparison group. In these samples, Tu-stroma did a better job than CA125 of telling people with Stic apart from people who were healthy or had non-cancerous growths around the ovaries or fallopian tubes.

There’s an important catch. The researchers were working with samples from people whose diagnoses were already known. Only a small number had Stic, so the results are still uncertain. If the test were offered widely to people without symptoms, very few would be likely to have these patches of abnormal cells. Even a small proportion of false alarms could send many people for unnecessary tests or even surgery.
What it could mean for people at higher risk

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are genes that help repair damage to DNA, the genetic instructions in our cells. People who inherit a harmful change in either gene have a higher risk of ovarian cancer. They may be advised to consider surgery to remove their ovaries and fallopian tubes once they have finished having children or if they do not plan to have them. The operation lowers their risk, but it ends their ability to get pregnant without fertility treatment. If they haven’t yet reached menopause, the sudden drop in hormones after surgery brings it on straight away.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) advises that specialist teams can consider regular CA125 testing for some people at high inherited risk who delay or decline surgery. Tu-stroma might one day improve that monitoring. For now, even if the experimental test picks up no warning signs, that result gives someone no basis to postpone recommended surgery.

A large UK trial found that screening with CA125 picked up more ovarian and fallopian tube cancers at an early stage. Even after years of follow-up, there was no clear evidence that fewer people died from those cancers. With Tu-stroma, researchers still need to find out how often the abnormal cells in the tube lining start growing into nearby tissue. They also need to work out what to do if the blood test flags a problem but a scan shows nothing. The question a screening trial would ultimately have to answer is whether acting on that result saves lives.

articles.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
articles.author: Li Li (李黎), Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Penn State
paras: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “blue baby syndrome.”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate concentrations, even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.
The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.
The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.
We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.

That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, particularly those using well water.

Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, including certain cancers and adverse birth outcomes, such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied.
We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.

Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up most of the global river networks, have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.
Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also fuel algal growth and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.

A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or treated before they drink it. Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.
To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households.

Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, conventional methods remove little nitrate. Removing it requires specialized technologies that can be costly to operate.

Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?

Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.
